In [[computer science]], '''coinduction''' is a technique for defining and proving properties of systems of [[concurrency (computer science)|concurrent]] interacting [[object (computing)|object]]s.

Coinduction is the [[mathematic]]al [[dual (category theory)|dual]] to [[structural induction]].{{citation needed|date=January 2023}} Coinductively defined [[data type]]s are known as '''codata''' and are typically [[Infinity|infinite]] [[data structures]], such as [[stream (computing)|streams]].

As a definition or [[specification (computing)|specification]], coinduction describes how an object may be "observed", "broken down" or "destructed" into simpler objects. As a [[proof (math)|proof]] technique, it may be used to show that an equation is satisfied by all possible [[implementation (computing)|implementation]]s of such a specification.

To generate and manipulate codata, one typically uses [[corecursion|corecursive]] functions, in conjunction with [[lazy evaluation]].  Informally, rather than defining a function by pattern-matching on each of the inductive constructors, one defines each of the "destructors" or "observers" over the function result.

In programming, co-logic programming (co-LP for brevity) "is a natural generalization of [[logic programming]] and coinductive logic programming, which in turn generalizes other extensions of logic programming, such as infinite trees, lazy predicates, and concurrent communicating predicates. Co-LP has applications to rational trees, verifying infinitary properties, lazy evaluation, [[concurrent logic programming]], [[model checking]], [[bisimilarity]] proofs, etc."<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://lambda-the-ultimate.org/node/2513|title = Co-Logic Programming &#124; Lambda the Ultimate}}</ref> Experimental implementations of co-LP are available from the [[University of Texas at Dallas]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.utdallas.edu/~gupta/|title = Gopal Gupta's Home Page}}</ref> and in the language [[Logtalk]] (for examples see  <ref>{{Cite web|url=https://github.com/LogtalkDotOrg/logtalk3/tree/master/examples/coinduction|title = Logtalk3/Examples/Coinduction at master · LogtalkDotOrg/Logtalk3|website = [[GitHub]]}}</ref>) and [[SWI-Prolog]].

== Description ==
In his book ''Types and Programming Languages'',<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262303828/types-and-programming-languages/|title = Types and Programming Languages|first=Benjamin C. |last=Pierce|author-link = Benjamin C. Pierce|publisher = MIT Press}}</ref> [[Benjamin C. Pierce]] gives a concise statement of both the ''principle of induction'' and the ''principle of coinduction''.  While this article is not primarily concerned with ''induction'', it is useful to consider their somewhat generalized forms at once.  In order to state the principles, a few preliminaries are required.

=== Preliminaries ===

Let <math>U</math> be a set and <math>F</math> be a [[Monotonic function#In order theory|monotone function]] <math>2^U \rightarrow 2^U</math>, that is:

<math display="block"> X \subseteq Y \Rightarrow F(X) \subseteq F(Y) </math>

Unless otherwise stated, <math>F</math> will be assumed to be monotone.

* ''X'' is ''F-closed'' if <math>F(X) \subseteq X </math>
* ''X'' is ''F-consistent'' if <math>X \subseteq F(X) </math>
* ''X'' is a [[Fixed point (mathematics)#Fixed points of partial orders|fixed point]] if <math>X = F(X) </math>

These terms can be intuitively understood in the following way.  Suppose that <math>X</math> is a set of assertions, and <math>F(X)</math> is the operation that yields the consequences of <math>X</math>. Then <math>X</math> is ''F-closed'' when one cannot conclude any more than has already been asserted, while <math>X</math> is ''F-consistent'' when all of the assertions are supported by other assertions (i.e. there are no "non-''F''-logical assumptions").

The [[Knaster–Tarski theorem]] tells us that the ''least fixed-point'' of <math>F</math> (denoted <math>\mu F</math>) is given by the intersection of all ''F-closed'' sets, while the ''greatest fixed-point'' (denoted <math>\nu F</math>) is given by the union of all ''F-consistent'' sets.  We can now state the principles of induction and coinduction.

=== Definition ===

* ''Principle of induction'': If <math>X</math> is ''F-closed'', then <math>\mu F \subseteq X</math>
* ''Principle of coinduction'': If <math>X</math> is ''F-consistent'', then <math>X \subseteq \nu F</math>

== Discussion ==

The principles, as stated, are somewhat opaque, but can be usefully thought of in the following way.  Suppose you wish to prove a property of <math>\mu F</math>.  By the ''principle of induction'', it suffices to exhibit an ''F-closed'' set <math>X</math> for which the property holds.  Dually, suppose you wish to show that <math>x \in \nu F</math>.  Then it suffices to exhibit an ''F-consistent'' set that <math>x</math> is known to be a member of.

== Examples ==

=== Defining a set of data types ===
{{see also|Data type}}
Consider the following grammar of datatypes:

<math display="block"> T = \bot \;|\;\top \;|\; T \times T </math>

That is, the set of types includes the "bottom type" <math>\bot</math>, the "top type" <math>\top</math>, and product types.  These types can be identified with strings over the alphabet <math>\Sigma = \{\bot, \top, \times\}</math>.  Let <math>\Sigma^{\leq \omega}</math> denote all (possibly infinite) strings over <math>\Sigma</math>.  Consider the function <math>F: 2^{\Sigma^{\leq \omega}} \rightarrow 2^{\Sigma^{\leq \omega}}</math>:

<math display="block"> F(X) = \{\bot, \top\} \cup \{ x \times y : x,y \in X \} </math>

In this context, <math>x \times y</math> means "the concatenation of string <math>x</math>, the symbol <math>\times</math>, and string <math>y</math>."  We should now define our set of datatypes as a fixpoint of <math>F</math>, but it matters whether we take the ''least'' or ''greatest'' fixpoint.

Suppose we take <math>\mu F</math> as our set of datatypes.  Using the ''principle of induction'', we can prove the following claim:

{{block indent| All datatypes in <math>\mu F</math> are ''finite''}}

To arrive at this conclusion, consider the set of all finite strings over <math>\Sigma</math>.  Clearly <math>F</math> cannot produce an infinite string, so it turns out this set is ''F-closed'' and the conclusion follows.

Now suppose that we take <math>\nu F</math> as our set of datatypes.  We would like to use the ''principle of coinduction'' to prove the following claim:

{{block indent| The type <math>\bot \times \bot \times \cdots \in \nu F</math>}}

Here <math>\bot \times \bot \times \cdots </math> denotes the infinite string <math>(\bot, \times, \bot, \times, \ldots)</math>.  To use the ''principle of coinduction'', consider the set:

<math display="block"> S = \{\bot,\; \bot \times \bot \times \cdots \} </math>

This set is ''F-consistent''.  First, <math>\bot \in \{\bot, \top\} \subseteq F(S)</math>.  Second, since <math>\bot \in S</math> and <math>\bot \times \bot \times \cdots \in S</math>, we have <math>\bot \times (\bot \times \bot \times \cdots) \in F(S)</math>.  Interpreting strings as [[Sequence#Formal definition and basic properties|sequences]] (functions from <math>\mathbb{N} \rightarrow \Sigma</math>), prepending the finite prefix <math>\bot \times</math> to the infinite string <math>\bot \times \bot \times \cdots</math> yields <math>\bot \times \bot \times \cdots</math> itself, so <math>\bot \times \bot \times \cdots \in F(S)</math>.  Therefore <math>S \subseteq F(S)</math>, and by the ''principle of coinduction'', <math>\bot \times \bot \times \cdots \in \nu F</math>.

'''Note.'''  The representation of types as strings over <math>\Sigma</math> is not faithful to the underlying tree structure.  Finite strings such as <math>\bot \times \top \times \bot</math> are ambiguous without bracketing, and for any infinite string <math>s</math> the concatenation <math>s \times t = s</math> for all <math>t</math>, so distinct trees may be identified.  This does not affect the argument above, which only illustrates the ''principle of coinduction'' via ''F''-consistency, but it would matter in settings where constructor structure must be preserved.  A standard structural treatment represents types via the isomorphism <math>T \cong 1 + 1 + (T \times T)</math>; see [[F-coalgebra]] for details.

=== Coinductive datatypes in programming languages ===

Consider the following definition of a [[Stream (computing)|stream]] in [[Haskell]]:<ref>{{Cite CiteSeerX|title = Practical Coinduction|first1=Dexter |last1=Kozen|author1-link =  Dexter Kozen |first2=Alexandra |last2=Silva |author2-link=Alexandra Silva | citeseerx=10.1.1.252.3961 }}</ref>

<syntaxhighlight lang="haskell">
data Stream a = S a (Stream a)

-- Stream "destructors"
head :: Stream a -> a
head (S a astream) = a
tail :: Stream a -> Stream a
tail (S a astream) = astream
</syntaxhighlight>

The first line says that a stream is made up of an element followed by a stream (S is a constructor of elements, and a denotes for an arbitrary type for the elements). As there is no [[Base case (induction)|base case]], this would seem to be a definition that is [[Non-well-founded set theory|not well-founded]], but it is nonetheless useful in programming and can be reasoned about.  In any case, a stream is an infinite list of elements from which you may observe the first element, or place an element in front of to get another stream.

=== Relationship with ''F''-coalgebras ===
{{further|F-coalgebra}}
Consider the [[Functor#endofunctor|endofunctor]] <math>F</math> in the [[category of sets]]:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
F(x) &= A \times x \\
F(f) &= \langle \mathrm{id}_A, f \rangle 
\end{align}</math>

The ''final F-coalgebra'' <math>\nu F</math> has the following morphism associated with it:

<math display="block"> \mathrm{out}: \nu F \rightarrow F(\nu F) = A \times \nu F </math>

This induces another coalgebra <math>F(\nu F)</math> with associated morphism <math>F(\mathrm{out})</math>.  Because <math>\nu F</math> is ''final'', there is a unique morphism

<math display="block"> \overline{F(\mathrm{out})}: F(\nu F) \rightarrow \nu F </math>

such that

<math display="block"> \mathrm{out} \circ \overline{F(\mathrm{out})} = F\left(\overline{F(\mathrm{out})}\right) \circ F(\mathrm{out}) 
= F\left(\overline{F(\mathrm{out})} \circ \mathrm{out}\right)</math>

The composition <math>\overline{F(\mathrm{out})} \circ \mathrm{out}</math> induces another ''F''-coalgebra homomorphism <math>\nu F \rightarrow \nu F</math>.  Since <math>\nu F</math> is final, this homomorphism is unique and therefore <math>\mathrm{id}_{\nu F}</math>.  Altogether we have:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\overline{F(\mathrm{out})} \circ \mathrm{out}
&= \mathrm{id}_{\nu F} \\[0.5ex]
\mathrm{out} \circ \overline{F(\mathrm{out})}
= F\bigl(\overline{F(\mathrm{out})} \circ \mathrm{out}\bigr)
&= \mathrm{id}_{F(\nu F)}
\end{align}
</math>

This witnesses the isomorphism <math>\nu F \simeq F(\nu F)</math>, which in categorical terms indicates that <math>\nu F</math> is a fixed point of <math>F</math> and justifies the notation.<ref>{{Cite book|chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-32202-0_2|chapter = Generic Programming with Adjunctions|first = Ralf |last=Hinze| title=Generic and Indexed Programming |publisher = Springer| series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science | year=2012 | volume=7470 | pages=47–129 | doi=10.1007/978-3-642-32202-0_2 | isbn=978-3-642-32201-3 }}</ref>{{verify inline|reason=This was previously rather generically placed at the start. Unclear what exactly it was supporting|date=March 2025}}

==== Stream as a final coalgebra ====

We will show that <code>Stream A</code> is the final coalgebra of the functor <math>F(x) = A \times x</math>.  Consider the following implementations:

<syntaxhighlight lang="haskell">
out astream = (head astream, tail astream)
out' (a, astream) = S a astream
</syntaxhighlight>

These are easily seen to be mutually inverse, witnessing the isomorphism.  See the reference for more details.

=== Relationship with mathematical induction ===
{{further|Mathematical induction}}
We will demonstrate how the ''principle of induction'' subsumes mathematical induction.
Let <math>P</math> be some property of [[natural numbers]].  We will take the following definition of mathematical induction:

<math display="block">0 \in P \and (n \in P \Rightarrow n+1 \in P) \Rightarrow \mathbb{N} \subseteq P</math>

Now consider the function <math>F: 2^{\mathbb{N}} \rightarrow 2^{\mathbb{N}}</math>:

<math display="block">F(X) = \{0\} \cup \{x + 1 : x \in X \}</math>

It should not be difficult to see that <math>\mu F = \mathbb{N}</math>.  Therefore, by the ''principle of induction'', if we wish to prove some property <math>P</math> of <math>\mathbb{N}</math>, it suffices to show that <math>P</math> is ''F-closed''.  In detail, we require:

<math display="block">F(P) \subseteq P</math>

That is,

<math display="block">\{0\} \cup \{x + 1 : x \in P \} \subseteq P </math>

This is precisely ''mathematical induction'' as stated.
